meta.descriptionEn: On 6 November 1986, a giant Chinook helicopter carrying oil workers home from the Brent field was just minutes from landing at Sumburgh in the Shetland Islands. Then the crew heard a bang. Within moments the aircraft had broken apart in the air and fallen into the North Sea. Only two people survived. How could a modern, trusted helicopter fail so suddenly? What was hidden inside its gearbox? And how did the search teams recover the wreckage from 90 metres of rough water to find the answer? This documentary follows the flight, the rescue, the underwater recovery and the investigation, and shows how the tragedy changed helicopter safety and offshore travel.
meta.descriptionUr: 6 November 1986 ko Brent oilfield se wapas aa raha ek bara Chinook helicopter Shetland ke Sumburgh airport se sirf chand minute door tha. Achanak crew ne ek zor ka dhamaka suna aur helicopter hawa mein toot kar North Sea mein gir gaya. Sirf do log zinda bache. Aisa kyun hua? Gearbox ke andar kya chhupa tha? Is documentary mein parwaz, rescue, samundar se malba nikalne aur tehqiqat ki poori kahani dekhein, aur jaanein ke is hadse ne helicopter safety ko kaise badal diya.

articleEn: On 6 November 1986, a large Chinook helicopter was bringing workers back from the Brent oilfield to the Shetland Islands. It was a Boeing-Vertol Model 234LR, and its destination was Sumburgh Airport. The runway was almost within reach. Then, just 2.5 miles (4 kilometres) short of it, a catastrophic failure suddenly occurred in the helicopter's forward transmission. The failure made the two rotor blades collide. The Chinook had two rotors, one at the front and one at the back. The helicopter fell into the sea and sank very quickly.

Forty-three passengers and two crew members died, 45 people in all. Only two people survived, one passenger and one crew member, and both were injured. The accident was investigated by Britain's Air Accidents Investigation Branch, known as the AAIB.

Consider it for a moment: an ordinary trip home turned into a major disaster within moments, and many questions were left behind. First, what failed so suddenly in such a strong helicopter? Second, how were the survivors found after the crash into the sea? Third, what changed after the accident? In this article we follow the story from the beginning and arrive at the investigators' findings.

articleEn: The Chinook's story begins in 1957, when the company Vertol started work on a new tandem-rotor helicopter. It was called the Model 107. At the time, the American Army wanted to replace its old piston-engine Sikorsky CH-37 Mojave with a new gas-turbine helicopter. In June 1958 the Army ordered a few V-107s from Vertol and named them YHC-1A. But many Army officers found the machine too heavy for assault work and too light for general transport. So the decision changed. The Marines later adopted the YHC-1A as the CH-46 Sea Knight, while the Army asked for a larger version of the V-107, which the company called the Model 114.

The Model 114 made its first flight on 21 September 1961. In 1962 it was designated the CH-47A, and it was named Chinook after the Chinook people, who are native to the Pacific Northwest of America. Interestingly, Boeing had bought Vertol in 1960.

The most distinctive feature of its design is the pair of rotors, one at the front and one at the back. They turn in opposite directions, which is called counter-rotating. Because of this arrangement, no separate antitorque tail rotor is needed, so all of the engine power can be used for lift and speed. If one engine fails, the other can drive both rotors. The helicopter also stays more stable when cargo is dropped or picked up. Its top speed is 170 knots, or 310 kilometres per hour, which was quite fast compared with other utility helicopters of the 1960s. Improved versions followed over time, such as the CH-47D, which had more powerful engines and composite rotor blades. Our sources give different years for its entry into service, some saying 1982 and some 1979.

Now to the civilian version. The CH-47C did not receive FAA approval for civil aviation because its hydraulic flight boost system was not redundant. That system was redesigned for the CH-47D, and so the aircraft could be certified under the name Boeing Model 234. The Model 234 was the civilian Chinook. Besides carrying passengers and cargo, it was used for aerial firefighting, logging, construction and the oil-extraction industry.

The helicopter at Sumburgh was a Model 234LR, the long-range version, which could be used for all-passenger, all-cargo or mixed work. In December 2006 Columbia Helicopters bought the Model 234 type certificate from Boeing. Today the surviving aircraft do heavy-lift work with Columbia. In other words, the machine that once carried passengers to offshore platforms now does non-passenger work. But why did that happen?

articleEn: Let us turn to Sumburgh Airport. It is the main airport of the Shetland Islands, located in the parish of Dunrossness at the southern end of the Mainland. It is 20 miles south of Lerwick, though by road the distance is given as 25 miles, or 40 kilometres. The airport's history begins in 1936. Captain E. E. Fresson of Highland Airways surveyed Sumburgh Links and had grass strips laid. The airport opened on 3 June 1936. The first flight came from Aberdeen in a De Havilland Dragon Rapide, flown by Fresson himself.

The weather here was a major problem. Low cloud and fog were frequent, and Sumburgh Head is close by. For this reason it was among the first airfields to have RDF facilities. Fresson proved to the Navy at Hatston that runways were necessary in winter. The RAF later adopted the same approach, and the site was used as RAF Sumburgh, which had three runways. No. 404 Squadron flew Beaufighters from here, attacking Axis shipping near the Norwegian coast. Two of the three old runways are still in use today.

The airport has some unusual features. Instead of an ordinary helipad, it has a 550-metre helicopter runway. Another oddity is that the western end of runway 09/27 crosses the A970 road, and the level-crossing barriers are closed for every flight.

The airport's records list several incidents. On 31 July 1979 a Dan-Air oil industry support flight ran off the end of the runway into the sea. According to the investigation, the cause was that the elevator gust-lock had re-engaged, so the aircraft could not climb into the air. On 23 August 2013 a CHC Super Puma AS332 L2 crashed 2 miles west of the airport, and 4 people died. The UK's AAIB named the lack of effective monitoring of flight instruments as one cause of that accident.

But our story is from 1986. The Brent oilfield lay in the East Shetland Basin, and a helicopter shuttle service was being run for it. This Chinook normally stayed at Aberdeen Airport. But from 3 November 1986 it was stationed at Sumburgh so that the Brent field shuttle could run, only three days before the accident. So Sumburgh was the Chinook's new base, and this Brent trip was part of that shuttle. The stage was set: an airport, a new shuttle and a large Chinook. Next we meet the crew and the morning of 6 November.

articleEn: Let us go to the morning of 6 November 1986. First, we meet the two pilots flying this Chinook. The captain was Pushp Vaid. He was 45 years old and a former Indian Air Force pilot. He had joined British International Helicopters in 1975 and had been flying the Chinook since 1982. So Captain Vaid was no novice. He had spent eleven years with the company, and this heavy tandem-rotor machine was familiar to him.

In the co-pilot's seat sat First Officer Neville Nixon, aged 43. His story was a little different. He had worked for Bristow Helicopters but left that job because he wanted to help run his wife's chemist's shop. Imagine a pilot leaving the sky to look after a shop. But the sky called him back. He returned to flying and was now working with British International Helicopters. So the two men in the cockpit were an experienced captain and a first officer who had returned to flying after a break.

Now to the morning itself. On 6 November the Chinook's first flight was delayed because of an oil leak from the engine gearbox. According to the source, the leak was fixed quickly. The cause of the accident turned out to be different: a gear in the forward transmission, which we will come to later.

The Chinook then took off from Sumburgh at 08:58 with 40 passengers on board, bound for the Brent field. The shuttle carried workers to and from the Brent oilfield. That day, too, passengers and goods were exchanged. The aircraft visited three platforms, and at each one freight and passengers were swapped, with some people getting off and others getting on. Finally, the Chinook took off from Brent Platform C at 10:22 and headed back toward Sumburgh. So from 08:58 to 10:22, about an hour and 24 minutes, the Chinook had made a round of three platforms.

This time there were 44 passengers on board, plus three crew members, two pilots and a flight attendant, 47 people in all. Everyone was heading for Sumburgh. One small note: the sources do not say how many people changed at which platform, but the number of passengers had gone from 40 to 44.

The Chinook was cruising at 2,500 feet. Open sea lay below, and the Shetland coast was ahead. It was an ordinary day, an ordinary shuttle, and everything routine. But very soon this day would change forever. What happened in the cockpit as the aircraft neared Sumburgh? In the next chapter we move toward that moment.

articleEn: Now we come to the moment that changed everything. The Chinook was approaching Sumburgh, and everything seemed routine. It had been cruising at 2,500 feet. As Sumburgh came closer, it was cleared to descend, down to 1,000 feet, about 300 metres. The Chinook was now getting quite close to the sea.

The Chinook then reported by radio that it was 4.5 miles from the airfield, about 7.2 kilometres. In reply, the controller cleared it to land on helicopter runway 24. Remember that Sumburgh has a separate runway for helicopters, not a pad. This runway is only 550 metres long, or 1,804 feet, and the Chinook was heading for it.

And then? Silence. The source says only that nothing more was heard. No other radio message was received. There was silence, while something had gone badly wrong above the sea. According to the source, the report was made at 4.5 miles and the failure occurred at 2.5 miles, so a gap of about two miles lay in between.

What had happened? The answer is found in the cockpit voice recorder. It shows that the crew first noticed increasing noise on the flightdeck. After that noise came a bang, a sound like an explosion. The voice recorder preserves this order. What lay behind the bang? According to the source, a catastrophic failure had occurred in the Chinook's forward transmission.

The Chinook has two large rotors, one at the front and one at the back. The two must turn together in a precise sequence, which is called synchronisation. When the synchronisation was lost, the blades of the two rotors collided. All of this happened in the air, over the sea. These details came out of the investigation by the AAIB, the Air Accidents Investigation Branch. We will look at them further later.

The crew made a last attempt to respond. According to the voice recorder, they applied full cyclic pitch control, using the control that steers the helicopter to its full extent. But the aircraft did not respond. The controls no longer had any effect, and the pilots had lost control of the machine. The helicopter began to fall toward the sea from about 150 feet, roughly 50 metres, about the height of a tall building.

The damage did not end as it fell. A large part of the helicopter had already broken up in the air from the colliding rotor blades. It then hit the sea and sank very quickly. The spot was only 2.5 miles east of the airport, or 4 kilometres.

Think about it. The destination was only two and a half miles away, yet for the 47 people on board that distance suddenly became very long. The question was whether anyone in the sea had survived. At that very moment another helicopter was flying nearby, and its story is in the next chapter.

articleEn: At that moment there was another helicopter in the sky. It was a Coastguard Sikorsky S-61, which had just left Sumburgh on a training flight. Consider the coincidence: a search and rescue crew, normally on standby for accidents, happened to be near the area. Soon they spotted liferafts in the sea and reported it. Now all eyes were on the water.

The crew then saw a person clinging to a large piece of wreckage. This was the first survivor. The rescue crew pulled him up into the helicopter by winch. This work is done by hovering the helicopter over the water. During this, the crew spotted another survivor among the other victims swimming in the water. So two people were found alive that morning. One was a passenger, and the other was Captain Pushp Vaid, a member of the flight crew. The source does not say whether the person clinging to the wreckage was the passenger or the captain. All that is known is that both were taken into the helicopter.

After this the crew looked around the area, but no further signs of survivors appeared. Time was now very precious. The Coastguard helicopter set off with the two injured people for Lerwick, from where they were to be moved to hospital. Sumburgh Airport is about 20 miles south of Lerwick, and by road the distance is 25 miles, or 40 kilometres.

Meanwhile, the search continued at sea. It was carried out by air and by water, in case anyone else could be found. But the search found no further survivors. This is the point where the saddest fact of that day emerges. All those found on the surface of the water were taken out and brought to the airport. Out of respect, we will not go into further detail on this.

In this accident 45 people died: 43 passengers and two crew members, while only two survived. Among the crew who died were First Officer Neville Nixon and the flight attendant. We remember them all with respect.

One more point. Sumburgh Airport is still a base for helicopter operators such as the Coastguard, Bristow and Babcock, who carry out SAR and crew-change work. Sumburgh had seen a disaster before. In 1979 Dan-Air Flight 0034 went off the end of the runway into the sea, and 17 people died.

But when the search for survivors ended on that day in 1986, a new question arose: where was the Chinook's wreckage, and why had it fallen? The answer lay in the depths of the sea. In the next chapter we see how the wreck was found.

articleEn: At 09:00 on the morning of 7 November 1986, a diving support vessel, MSV Deepwater 1, began searching for the sunken wreckage. Only one night had passed since the accident. The ship is now named Rockwater 1. The sea was in poor condition, the tidal currents were very strong, and the water was about 90 metres deep. Finding anything at such a depth is not easy. Still, the search succeeded and the wreck was found.

But the real test came after that. The problem was that Deepwater 1 was a monohulled vessel. In rising waves and strong current, it struggled to hold its position. Imagine working 90 metres down while the ship above keeps moving. A second, more stable vessel was needed.

Then Shell Expro's Multi Services Vessel, MSV Stadive, arrived at the scene and took over as the primary recovery vessel. Stadive was a semi-submersible, and for this reason it was able to bring up the important parts very quickly. This difference proved very important.

By the evening of 10 November, the most important items for the investigators had been recovered from the sea. These were, first of all, the cockpit voice recorder, then the cockpit section of the fuselage. The rotors and rotor heads were also brought up, along with the gearboxes and the control systems connected to them. These were the parts that might hold the secret of the accident.

All these items were transferred to Deepwater 1. That vessel then headed for Aberdeen so that the material could be sent on. The destination was the Air Accidents Investigation Branch, the AAIB, the body that was to carry out the detailed analysis of these parts. Consider the task: on one side were a rough sea and strong currents, on the other a depth of 90 metres. Yet within a few days the key parts had come up.

Meanwhile Stadive stayed where it was. It recovered most of the rest of the fuselage and also continued the recovery of the victims. Of the 45 victims in total, 44 were recovered from the sea. This was a very serious and sad part of the whole operation.

One thing should be remembered here. The purpose of raising the wreckage was not merely to collect pieces of the helicopter. The purpose was to find out what had actually happened. This whole operation was the teamwork of two vessels. One found the wreck and sent the key parts to Aberdeen, while the other handled most of the recovery in difficult conditions.
Now the parts were ready for the AAIB's analysis. The question was which part had failed first. In the next chapter we find out.

articleEn: What exactly broke inside the Chinook so that it came apart in the air? The AAIB's answer fits in one sentence, but a long story lies behind it. The accident was caused by the failure of a modified bevel ring gear in the forward transmission. When this gear failed, the synchronisation of the helicopter's two rotors was lost.

The Chinook has two large rotors, at the front and at the back, in what is called a tandem layout. They must stay in very precise step with each other. When that coordination broke, the rotor blades collided. For this reason the helicopter suffered severe break-up in the air. According to the voice recorder, the crew first noticed increasing noise on the flightdeck and then heard a bang. Despite applying full cyclic pitch control, the aircraft did not respond. The investigation found that the accident was caused by the failure of the gear, and that when synchronisation was lost, the rotor blades collided.

Now the real question: why did the gear fail? The AAIB said there were two underlying causes. First, a previously approved test programme was inadequate. Second, a stringent inspection programme was unable to do its job. In other words, there were two safety barriers, and neither worked on that day. The word modified is very important here. The same point is reflected in the AAIB's recommendations, that changes to vital components should be thoroughly checked before they are approved.

Now let us look at an older case. On 18 October 1974 a CH-47C on a delivery flight to Canada suffered a gear failure in its main combining gearbox. The cause of the accident was said to be a metallurgical flaw in the gear blank that had not been caught before machining. A drive shaft then failed as well. As a result, the rotors lost synchronisation and five people died. After a long legal process, the aircraft was later replaced.
Keep in mind that the two accidents were separate. The sources do not say that both had exactly the same cause. But what they share is the failure of a gear and the loss of synchronisation.

Here is another example. On 11 September 1982 a U.S. Army Chinook crashed at the Mannheim airshow, and 46 people were killed. There, lubrication had not reached the transmission bearings. The cause was a build-up of ground walnut shell grit, which was used for cleaning the machines. Its use was later stopped.
A lesson comes out of these events: even a small flaw in a vital part such as the transmission can become a danger to the whole aircraft.

The 1986 Chinook was a Boeing-Vertol Model 234LR. It was bringing workers back from the Brent oilfield and was only 2.5 miles from Sumburgh. So, in summary: a modified gear broke, synchronisation was lost, the rotors collided, and the helicopter fell into the sea. But a question remains: what did the world learn from this accident?

articleEn: After the accident, the AAIB made three recommendations. The first was that certification procedures be reviewed so that every modification to vital components is fully tested. The second was addressed to the Civil Aviation Authority. It asked how a specification for condition monitoring systems for helicopters could soon be included in the airworthiness requirements.

The third recommendation concerned the ADELT beacon, the Automatically Deployable Location Transmitter. On that day the beacon could not function because the rear part of the aircraft had suffered impact damage. For this reason, its location, crashworthiness, protection and power supply were to be reviewed again in the light of this accident.

The oil industry decided that the Chinook was too large for offshore support work. The remaining Chinooks were withdrawn and sold. In this way the Chinook disappeared from North Sea crew-servicing flights. Today the surviving aircraft do heavy-lift work with Columbia Helicopters, but without passengers.

The biggest lesson is that even a small change cannot be considered safe until it has been fully tested. In this accident 45 people died, and two survived. We should remember them, because behind every safety rule there is someone's sacrifice.

shorts.titleEn: 2.5 Miles From Home: The Sumburgh Chinook Tragedy of 1986
shorts.text: صرف 2.5 miles۔ بس اتنا فاصلہ باقی تھا، اور 45 لوگوں کی زندگی بدل گئی۔ 6 November 1986 کو ایک Chinook helicopter، Brent oilfield سے کارکنوں کو واپس لا رہا تھا۔ منزل تھی Sumburgh Airport، Shetland Islands میں۔ یہ Boeing-Vertol Model 234LR تھا۔ runway سے 2.5 miles، یعنی 4 kilometres پہلے، اس کے forward transmission میں اچانک بڑی خرابی آ گئی۔ Chinook کے دو rotors ہوتے ہیں، ایک آگے اور ایک پیچھے۔ خرابی کی وجہ سے دونوں rotor blades آپس میں ٹکرا گئے۔ helicopter سمندر میں جا گرا اور بہت جلد ڈوب گیا۔ اس حادثے میں 43 passengers اور 2 crew members جان سے گئے۔ صرف دو لوگ بچے۔ لیکن آخر transmission کے اندر ایسا کیا ٹوٹا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Sirf 2.5 miles. Bas itna fasla baqi tha, aur 45 logon ki zindagi badal gayi. 6 November 1986 ko ek Chinook helicopter, Brent oilfield se karkunon ko wapas la raha tha. Manzil thi Sumburgh Airport, Shetland Islands mein. Yeh Boeing-Vertol Model 234LR tha. runway se 2.5 miles, yani 4 kilometres pehle, is ke forward transmission mein achanak bari kharabi aa gayi. Chinook ke do rotors hotay hain, ek aage aur ek peechay. Kharabi ki wajah se dono rotor blades aapas mein takra gaye. helicopter samundar mein ja gira aur bohat jald doob gaya. Is hadsay mein 43 passengers aur 2 crew members jaan se gaye. Sirf do log bachay. Lekin aakhir transmission ke andar aisa kya toota tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 6 November 1986 a Chinook returning from the Brent oilfield crashed 2.5 miles from Sumburgh Airport.
A transmission failure made the rotor blades collide, and only two people survived.

shorts.titleEn: The Rescue Helicopter That Was Already in the Sky at Sumburgh
shorts.text: ایک helicopter گرا، اور اسی وقت قریب ہی ایک اور helicopter موجود تھا۔ کیا یہ صرف اتفاق تھا؟ یہ Coastguard کا Sikorsky S-61 تھا، جو Sumburgh سے ابھی ابھی ایک training flight پر روانہ ہوا تھا۔ جلد ہی crew نے سمندر میں liferafts دیکھیں اور اطلاع دی۔ پھر انہیں ایک شخص نظر آیا جو ملبے کے ایک بڑے ٹکڑے سے چمٹا ہوا تھا۔ یہ پہلا survivor تھا۔ crew نے winch کے ذریعے اسے اوپر helicopter میں کھینچ لیا۔ اسی دوران انہوں نے ایک اور survivor کو بھی دیکھا۔ مزید کوئی survivor نظر نہ آیا، تو دونوں کو Lerwick لے جایا گیا، جہاں سے hospital منتقل کیا گیا۔ air اور sea search بھی کی گئی۔ لیکن ایک بڑا سوال باقی تھا: ڈوبا ہوا ملبہ آخر کہاں تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek helicopter gira, aur usi waqt qareeb hi ek aur helicopter mojood tha. Kya yeh sirf ittefaq tha? Yeh Coastguard ka Sikorsky S-61 tha, jo Sumburgh se abhi abhi ek training flight par rawana hua tha. Jald hi crew ne samundar mein liferafts dekhein aur ittila di. Phir unhein ek shakhs nazar aaya jo malbay ke ek bare tukray se chimta hua tha. Yeh pehla survivor tha. Crew ne winch ke zariye isay upar helicopter mein kheench liya. Isi dauran unhon ne ek aur survivor ko bhi dekha. Mazeed koi survivor nazar na aaya, to dono ko Lerwick le jaya gaya, jahan se hospital muntaqil kiya gaya. air aur sea search bhi ki gayi. Lekin ek bara sawal baqi tha: doobay hua malba aakhir kahan tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
A Coastguard Sikorsky S-61 had just left Sumburgh on a training flight when the Chinook went down.
Its crew spotted liferafts and winched the survivors aboard.

shorts.titleEn: Raising a Wreck From 90 Metres: The Race After the Chinook Crash
shorts.text: 90 metres گہرے سمندر میں ایک ملبہ چھپا تھا، اور حادثے کو بس ایک رات گزری تھی۔ 7 November 1986 کو صبح 09:00 بجے diving support vessel MSV Deepwater 1 نے تلاش شروع کی۔ سمندر کی حالت خراب تھی اور tidal currents بہت تیز تھے۔ پھر بھی ملبہ مل گیا۔ لیکن مسئلہ یہ تھا کہ Deepwater 1 ایک monohulled جہاز تھا، اور بڑھتی لہروں میں اپنی جگہ پر رہنا مشکل ہو رہا تھا۔ پھر Shell Expro کا MSV Stadive پہنچا۔ یہ semi-submersible تھا، اس لیے اس نے اہم حصے جلدی نکال لیے۔ 10 November کی شام تک cockpit voice recorder، rotors اور gearboxes نکالے جا چکے تھے۔ یہ سب Aberdeen بھیجا گیا، تجزیے کے لیے۔ تو AAIB کو ان میں سے کیا ملا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: 90 metres gehray samundar mein ek malba chhupa tha, aur hadsay ko bas ek raat guzri thi. 7 November 1986 ko subah 09:00 bajay diving support vessel MSV Deepwater 1 ne talash shuru ki. Samundar ki halat kharab thi aur tidal currents bohat tez thay. Phir bhi malba mil gaya. Lekin masla yeh tha ke Deepwater 1 ek monohulled jahaz tha, aur barhti lehron mein apni jagah par rehna mushkil ho raha tha. Phir Shell Expro ka MSV Stadive pohancha. Yeh semi-submersible tha, is liye is ne aham hissay jaldi nikal liye. 10 November ki shaam tak cockpit voice recorder, rotors aur gearboxes nikalay ja chukay thay. Yeh sab Aberdeen bheja gaya, tajziye ke liye. To AAIB ko in mein se kya mila? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
After the 1986 Chinook crash, vessels searched 90 metres of rough water for the wreck.
The MSV Stadive recovered the voice recorder, rotors and gearboxes for AAIB analysis.
